name: Intellectual property
summary: Intellectual property is the view that creations of the mind (inventions, writings, designs, marks) should be held as property-like exclusive rights that their creators or owners can enforce against others, for a limited or unlimited time. Its defenders ground this in incentives to innovate, in labour and desert, or in the creator's personality; its critics hold that such exclusive rights are monopolies that hinder innovation and access to knowledge.
scope: The body of ideas about whether and why creations of the mind (patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets and the like) should be treated as property, as Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (s1), WIPO (s2) and the legal and scholarly works (s4, s5, s6) set it out: the personality-based, utilitarian and Lockean justifications for exclusive rights, and the critics' case (monopoly, enclosure of the commons, access to knowledge, libertarian objections) that the same sources record as part of the debate. It covers the positions those sources attribute to the idea of IP and to its critics; where they take opposite sides on a question it is a split. It excludes the technical doctrine of any one national IP statute, and the programmes of individual firms, lobbies or parties.
